entry.title: I Built a Lightweight Python RAG Orchestrator That Works with SQLite, PGVector and Qdrant
entry.summary:
Most RAG frameworks today assume: a huge dependency graph mandatory LLM orchestration opinionated pipelines complex configuration But many real-world systems need something simpler. Especially when: you already have an existing pipeline you want local/offline execution you need predictable retrieval you do not want every step delegated to an LLM So I built rag-orchestrator. The project was designed around one key idea: RAG infrastructure should be modular, lightweight, and database-agnostic. The orchestrator supports: SQLite PGVector Qdrant through an abstract storage layer. This means you can switch backends without rebuilding the whole pipeline. The project provides abstraction layers for: Embeddings Retrievers Cleaners Vector stores Processing steps You can easily plug in: your own embedding provider your own retriever custom preprocessing logic external pipelines without rewriting internal logic. One important design decision: The orchestrator works without an LLM for almost the entire pipeline. LLMs are only required at a single step where they actually add value. This makes the system: cheaper faster more deterministic easier to debug The module intentionally requires very few input parameters. The goal was: fast onboarding simple integration production-friendly defaults The repository already includes: integration tests runnable scripts usage examples You can inspect them directly in the scripts/ directory. The project was built to integrate into: existing RAG pipelines enterprise systems AI backends local AI stacks internal search systems instead of forcing users into a completely new ecosystem. ```bash id="1b38r0"
## Why this matters
A lot of modern RAG tooling is becoming increasingly framework-heavy.
But many production systems actually need:
* predictability * portability * low overhead * composability
rather than autonomous agent complexity.
This project focuses exactly on that.

entry.summary: For a quarter century, the Google search box has been one of the most recognizable interfaces in computing: a thin white rectangle, a blinking cursor, a few typed words, and a list of blue links. On Tuesday, Google will formally retire that paradigm. At its annual I/O developer conference, Google announced a sweeping redesign of the search box itself — the literal text field where billions of queries begin every day — transforming it from a simple keyword input into a dynamic, AI-driven conversation starter that can accept text, images, PDFs, videos, and even open Chrome tabs as inputs.
